results.why: Deck B builds Rising Waters the proven way. Its twelve mana creatures, Mox Diamond and Quirion Ranger keep it casting spells while lands stay locked, and Opposition, Winter Orb, Port and Daze compound the denial. River Boa and Call of the Herd close the game quickly. Deck A's free spells do work under Waters, but its only real kill is a four-card Dreadnought/Stifle combo plus Black Vise, which makes it fragile and slow to win once the lock is set.

Deck A is the proven way to break Rising Waters' symmetry. Its 12 mana dorks plus Mox Diamond keep it casting spells while the opponent is locked on lands, and Opposition and Winter Orb compound the lock. River Boa and Call of the Herd close the game quickly. Deck B leans on free spells and Black Vise, which is cute, but its only real threat is 4 Stifle-dependent Dreadnoughts, so it often can't win once the lock is set.

Deck A assembles Mind Over Matter fast and redundantly. Dream Halls, Show and Tell, Intuition and the fast mana (Tomb, City of Traitors, Petal, Frantic Search) cheat out the 6-drops, then Arcanis and Kamahl loop into infinite cards and damage. Deck B is a slower draw-go deck that hard-casts six-mana pieces and wins with Stroke of Genius plus odd filler like Powder Keg, so it is less threatening and more vulnerable to aggression in Premodern.

Deck B is the proven Premodern Mind Over Matter shell: Dream Halls and Show and Tell cheat out the six-mana enchantment early, and fast mana plus Frantic Search, Meditate and Rush of Knowledge fuel the discard engine. Kamahl and Arcanis give it a clean untap-loop kill, and the mana base supports both the blue spells and the red finisher. Deck A is a slow hard-cast control pile that relies on resolving MoM at six mana and then Stroking, which is a much weaker, clunkier plan.

Deck B is a coherent mono-black Processor shell with clean mana. Dark Ritual, Lotus Petal and Ancient Tomb power out an early Processor, the discard pack protects it, and Negator, Specter and cheap removal support a fast, life-cheap game plan. Deck A is a scattered Tinker/Welder artifact pile with awkward colored mana, few true Processor synergies and unfocused one-ofs like Karn, Triskelion and Defense Grid, so it doesn't really build around Processor.

Deck A is the proven mono-black Processor shell. Dark Ritual, Lotus Petal, Ancient Tomb and City of Traitors power Processor out on turns 1-2, discard clears the way, and Negator and Specter give it a second threat axis with clean, consistent mana. Deck B has awkward mana (Lairs and Mox Diamond alongside City of Traitors), few real threats, and only loose synergy among Welder, Defense Grid and Processor, so the deck is less focused and less reliable.

Deck B builds the whole kill around Shapeshifter-as-Phage: two Wonders, Cephalid Pathmage, and Crafty Pathmage (activate it while Shapeshifter is still a 0/1, then discard Phage) give it evasion. Careful Study and Worldly Tutor reliably put Phage on top of the graveyard, and Rootwalla and Squee feed Survival. Deck A has only a single Wonder and Brawn for evasion, and spends slots on off-plan cards like Gilded Drake, Aquamoeba and Daze, so it is much less consistent at actually landing the Phage hit.

Deck B's discard engine of Merfolk Looter, Aquamoeba, Wild Mongrel and Survival reliably stacks Wonder and then Phage in the graveyard. Intuition gives it another way to set up the combo, and Gilded Drake and Daze are strong tempo support. Deck A plays an off-color Squee and Crafty Pathmage, which only works with awkward sequencing on a 4/4 Phage. Its Basking Rootwalla doesn't even reach the graveyard when madnessed, so its pieces are less coherent.

Deck A pairs Seismic Assault with a real recursion engine: Groundskeeper and Harvest Wurm return basic lands to keep feeding Assault, and Gamble tutors the enchantment. That makes the plan coherent and resilient, and it matches the established Premodern Terravore/Assault shell. Deck B's Wasteland and Fireblast are reasonable, but Krosan Tusker and 28 lands with no recursion make it a weaker, less focused Assault deck.

Deck B builds a real engine around Seismic Assault. Groundskeeper and Harvest Wurm recur basic lands as repeatable Assault ammo, and Gamble acts as extra copies of the key enchantment while dumping lands for Terravore. Deck A has more raw burn and Wasteland, but its colorless lands strain an RRR enchantment, and it lacks the recursion that turns Assault into a sustained machine gun.

Deck A runs 19 Forests plus 1 Cradle to maximize Rofellos' output, and it adds Survival of the Fittest as a real engine that turns spare creatures into a toolbox of Hermit, Masticore, Tusker, Baloth and Vigilante. Its full set of Sylvan Library and four Plow Under make the ramp payoff coherent. Deck B cuts Forests to 17 for three legendary Cradles, which weakens Rofellos and risks dead duplicate Cradles, and its tutoring relies on the weaker Worldly Tutor instead of Survival.

Deck B runs a full 4 Sylvan Library and 4 Plow Under, the core card advantage and lock pieces a Rofellos ramp deck wants. Survival of the Fittest gives it a real engine to find Masticore, Vigilante, Hermit or Tusker. Its 19 Forests also maximize Rofellos output, while Deck A spends slots on weaker filler like Worldly Tutor and Multani's Acolyte and cuts Library to two.

Deck B uses a real Legacy shell for a four-mana combo creature: Ancient Tomb, City of Traitors, Mox Diamond and Lotus Petal can land Salvagers or Karn on turns 1–2. It also has heavy redundancy for assembling LED plus a Ballista outlet: 4 Enlightened Tutor, 4 Tezzeret, Urza's Saga, and Agatha's Soul Cauldron as a second Salvagers. Deck A is a coherent blue tempo build, but it has only a few fast-mana sources for a 4-drop and slower, fairer card choices, so the combo comes online much later.

Deck A gives Salvagers real mana support. Ancient Tomb, City of Traitors, Mox Diamond and Lotus Petal can land the 4-drop on turns 1–2 and fund the {1}{W} loop. It also has layered ways to assemble LED and Ballista: Tezzeret, Karn wishing from the sideboard, Enlightened Tutor and Saga, with Cauldron as a backup route, all backed by real stax pieces. Deck B has good blue interaction, but its 4-mana combo creature sits awkwardly in a 19-land tempo shell with little acceleration and filler like Lórien Revealed, so it combos slowly and less reliably.

Deck B is the established mono-red Wildfire shell. Ancient Tomb, City of Traitors and 12 mana rocks reliably reach six mana by turns 3–4, and the rocks survive the Wildfire. Its finishers (Masticore, Covetous Dragon with plenty of artifacts, Rorix) live through the sweep, and the 16 Mountains easily support RR. Deck A has a cute Terravore angle, but only about 10 artifacts to keep Covetous Dragon alive, Birds that die to its own Wildfire, and a strained RR/GG mana base, so it is slower and less consistent.

Deck A is the proven mono-red Wildfire shell. Ancient Tomb, City of Traitors and 12 mana rocks can power out an early Wildfire while keeping its own artifact mana intact. That rock count also reliably supports Covetous Dragon and Masticore, and Pyroclasm, Earthquake and Bolt control the board before the Dragons and Hellion take over. Deck B's Terravore angle is cute, but it runs Covetous Dragon on only about 10 artifacts and its Birds die to its own Wildfire. It also has weaker acceleration and no sweepers to cover the early game.

Deck A follows the proven Premodern Wildfire shell. Mind Stone, Thran Dynamo and Mox Diamond survive Wildfire, so you stay ahead on mana after the sacrifice. Covetous Dragon and Masticore survive the 4 damage and win the post-Wildfire board. Deck B plays only one Dynamo and leans on Wall of Roots, which Wildfire kills, so it is really a land-destruction Ponza deck that breaks symmetry far worse after casting its namesake card.

Deck B is built like a real Wildfire deck. Its mana rocks (Mind Stone, three Thran Dynamo, Mox Diamond) survive its own Wildfire and let it cast the spell on turn 3–4. Its threats also outlive the sweep: Covetous Dragon has 5 toughness, Masticore can regenerate, and Terravore grows from the destroyed lands. Deck A has only one Dynamo and leans on Wall of Roots, which dies to Wildfire, so it plays more like a slower land-destruction pile with a weaker plan for after the sweep.

Deck A turns the combo into a real engine. Squandered Resources plus fetches and Mox Diamond fill graveyards with lands for Terravore. Natural Balance then rebuilds your mana while wrecking the opponent's, with Deed and discard supporting a proven Rock-style shell. Deck B's Drain Life plan is cute, but its mana dorks work against Natural Balance and its threat base is thin, so it's less focused and less powerful.

Deck B uses Squandered Resources and Natural Balance together with real payoffs. Mox Diamond, fetchlands and land sacrifice fill graveyards to grow Terravore into a huge trampler, and Natural Balance rebuilds your mana while wrecking the opponent's. Deck A's Drain Life finisher can work, but it is clunkier, relies on fragile mana dorks, and lacks the land-in-graveyard payoff that makes the pairing strong.

Deck B is the tighter UW Millstone control shell. Stroke of Genius doubles as card draw and an instant-speed kill once the opponent's library is low, and the extra Fact or Fiction, Disenchant and manlands give it more answers and more ways to close games. Deck A's two Ambassador Laquatus are a fragile three-mana creature engine in a deck already packing Wrath, and the extra narrow counters and third Brain Freeze add little over B's more flexible card choices.

Deck B commits harder to milling as a game plan. Ambassador Laquatus is a repeatable mana sink that ends games quickly in a control shell, and the third Brain Freeze adds lethal storm reach late. Deck A's Stroke of Genius and Vision Charm are weaker finishers, and B's Prohibit, extra Mana Leak and Dust Bowl round out a tighter counter-control mill list.

Deck B is closer to a tuned UW Millstone control list. It runs six counters (Counterspell plus Mana Leak) and five manlands as a backup win condition. Stroke of Genius and Vision Charm are flexible instant-speed finishers that don't clash with its own Wraths the way Ambassador Laquatus does in Deck A, and its single Powder Keg is less likely to blow up its own Millstones.

Deck A runs six counterspells instead of four, and its finishers fit a draw-go control shell: Stroke of Genius doubles as an instant-speed mill kill, and Vision Charm adds mill. The manlands give Standstill turns a backup clock. Deck B's Ambassador Laquatus is a fragile three-drop that clashes with its own Wraths, and its second Powder Keg and Dust Bowl add less than A's extra countermagic.

Deck A is truly built around Nether Spirit: the Spirit recurs every upkeep to feed Contamination, Innocent Blood, Diabolic Edict and Cabal Therapy flashback. Its only creature card is the Spirit, so Zombie Infestation discards never break the recursion, and Furnace and Scrying keep the graveyard clean. Its mono-black mana with Port and Wasteland also backs up the Contamination lock. Deck B is a reasonable WB control list, but there Nether Spirit is just a Wrath-resistant finisher rather than the engine, and its two-colour mana is shakier on BB, WW and WB costs.

Deck B is the real Nether Spirit engine deck. The recurring Spirit and Zombie tokens feed Contamination, Innocent Blood, Diabolic Edict and Cabal Therapy flashback, while Wasteland, Rishadan Port and Contamination lock the opponent's mana, and Furnace and Powder Keg keep the graveyard clean. Deck A is a reasonable W/B control shell, but Spirit is just a Wrath-proof threat there, and its split mana is shaky for both BB and WW.
